{{Short description|Topological subset with no isolated point}}

In [[general topology]], a subset <math>A</math> of a [[topological space]] is said to be '''dense-in-itself'''<ref>Steen & Seebach, p. 6</ref><ref>Engelking, p. 25</ref> or '''crowded'''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Levy |first1=Ronnie |last2=Porter |first2=Jack |title=On Two questions of Arhangel'skii and Collins regarding submaximal spaces |journal=Topology Proceedings |date=1996 |volume=21 |pages=143–154 |url=http://topology.nipissingu.ca/tp/reprints/v21/tp21008.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228597275 |last1=Dontchev |first1=Julian |last2=Ganster |first2=Maximilian |last3=Rose |first3=David |date=1977 |title=α-Scattered spaces II}}</ref>
if <math>A</math> has no [[isolated point]] of <math>A</math>.
Equivalently, <math>A</math> is dense-in-itself if every point of <math>A</math> is a [[limit point]] of <math>A</math>.
Thus <math>A</math> is dense-in-itself if and only if <math>A\subseteq A'</math>, where <math>A'</math> is the [[derived set (mathematics)|derived set]] of <math>A</math>.

A dense-in-itself [[closed set]] is called a [[perfect set]].  (In other words, a perfect set is a closed set without isolated point.)

The property of being dense-in-itself depends only on the [[subspace topology]] of <math>A</math>, namely, <math>A</math> is a dense-in-itself subset of <math>X</math> if and only if <math>A</math> is a dense-in-itself subset of <math>A</math>. Some authors would say that <math>A</math> is a perfect space in its subspace topology (note that the phrase ''perfect space'' is ambiguous).

The notion of [[dense set]] is distinct from ''dense-in-itself''.  This can sometimes be confusing, as "<math>X</math> is dense in <math>X</math>" (always true) is not the same as "<math>X</math> is dense-in-itself" (contains no isolated points).

==Examples==
A simple example of a set that is dense-in-itself but not closed (and hence not a perfect set) is the set of [[irrational numbers]] (considered as a subset of the [[real numbers]]). This set is dense-in-itself because every [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of an irrational number <math>x</math> contains at least one other irrational number <math>y \neq x</math>. On the other hand, the set of irrationals is not closed because every [[rational number]] lies in its [[closure (topology)|closure]]. Similarly, the set of rational numbers is also dense-in-itself but not closed in the space of real numbers.

The above examples, the irrationals and the rationals, are also [[dense set]]s in their topological space, namely <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. As an example that is dense-in-itself but not dense in its topological space, consider <math>\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]</math>. This set is not dense in <math>\mathbb{R}</math> but is dense-in-itself.

==Properties==
A [[singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] is never dense-in-itself.

The dense-in-itself subsets of any space are closed under arbitrary [[union of sets|unions]].<ref>Engelking, 1.7.10, p. 59</ref> In a dense-in-itself space, they include all [[open set]]s.<ref>Kuratowski, p. 78</ref> In a dense-in-itself [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] they include all [[dense set]]s.<ref>Kuratowski, p. 78</ref> However, spaces that are not T<sub>1</sub> may have dense subsets that are not dense-in-itself: for example in the dense-in-itself space <math>X=\{a,b\}</math> with the [[indiscrete topology]], the set <math>A=\{a\}</math> is dense, but is not dense-in-itself.

The closure of any dense-in-itself set is a [[perfect set]].<ref>Kuratowski, p. 77</ref>

In general, the [[intersection]] of two dense-in-itself sets is not dense-in-itself.  But the intersection of a dense-in-itself set and an open set is dense-in-itself.
